misconception.text: The angular speed of an object moving in a circle is the linear speed times the radius.

correction.text: The angular speed is the linear speed divided by the radius, so it is the same for every point on the rim.

signal.text: The paper offers the product of the linear speed and the radius as an option.

misconception.text: Centripetal acceleration pushes the object outward, away from the centre.

correction.text: It points inward. The inward acceleration is what keeps the object on the circle.

signal.text: Our own question offers the outward direction as an option.

misconception.text: Centripetal force is a new kind of force that pulls objects to the centre.

correction.text: It is the name for the net inward force, whatever provides it: gravity, tension or friction.

signal.text: Our own question offers the new force as an option.

misconception.text: A fluid flowing at a steady rate has no acceleration.

correction.text: A change in speed or direction is an acceleration, so the fluid is accelerating even at a steady rate.

signal.text: Our own teaching of the section, waiting for a paper question that shows the same mistake.

misconception.text: The Bernoulli effect explains why a curve ball curves.

correction.text: It explains the pressure difference between the two sides of a spinning ball, and the deflection of the air around it.

signal.text: Our own teaching of the section, waiting for a paper question that shows the same mistake.

misconception.text: The force opposing a body sliding down an incline is the friction alone.

correction.text: The component of the weight down the slope pushes against the motion as well, so the total opposing force is the friction plus that component.

signal.text: The paper offers the friction alone as an option, and the answer is the friction plus the component of the weight.

stem.text: A wheel of radius 0.5 m turns at 4 rad/s. What is the linear speed of a point on the rim?

explanation.text: The linear speed is v = ωr = 4 × 0.5 = 2 m/s.

stem.text: A car travels at 20 m/s round a circle of radius 50 m. What is its centripetal acceleration?

explanation.text: The centripetal acceleration is $a = v^2/r = 400/50 = 8$ m/s².

stem.text: A 1000 kg car goes round a bend of radius 100 m at 20 m/s. What centripetal force is needed?

explanation.text: The centripetal force is $F = mv^2/r = 1000 \times 400/100 = 4000$ N.

stem.text: A car travels at 20 m/s round a circle of radius 50 m. What is the centripetal acceleration?

explanation.text: The centripetal acceleration is $v^2/r = 400/50 = 8$ m/s², directed to the centre.

stem.text: A 1000 kg car goes round a bend of radius 100 m at 20 m/s. What centripetal force is needed?

explanation.text: The centripetal force is $F = mv^2/r = 1000 \times 400/100 = 4000$ N, supplied by the friction between the tyres and the road.

stem.text: A body slides on a horizontal surface at constant speed. The horizontal force applied to it is

options.text: equal in magnitude to the friction force

explanation.text: Constant speed means the net force is zero, so the applied force balances the friction exactly.
